overview:
Samavasaraṇa (Skt. *samavasaraṇa*, Prakrit *samavasaraṇa*) is the Jain term for the divinely manifested preaching assembly created for a Tīrthaṅkara immediately after attaining *kevala‑jñāna* (omniscience). It is not built by human hands; rather, it arises spontaneously through the workings of *puṇya* (merit) and cosmic order. All Jain traditions—Digambara, Śvetāmbara Mūrti‑pūjaka, Sthānakavāsī, and Terāpanth—affirm the concept, though they differ in descriptive details.

In classical Jain cosmology, the Samavasaraṇa is a perfectly symmetrical, circular, triple‑tiered structure. It is said to accommodate beings from all realms: humans, animals, celestial beings, and even infernal beings who momentarily experience peace. The Tīrthaṅkara sits at the center on a divine throne (*simhāsana*), facing all directions simultaneously without turning the body—a symbolic expression of non‑attachment and perfect equanimity. The assembly is arranged so that every listener perceives the Tīrthaṅkara as facing them directly.

The Samavasaraṇa is not merely an architectural or cosmological marvel; it is the moment when the *dharma‑tīrtha* (ford of liberation) becomes accessible. The Tīrthaṅkara delivers the *divya‑dhvani*—a transcendent, non‑verbal sound that each being understands in its own language. This teaching forms the basis of Jain scripture, ethical conduct, and the re‑establishment of the fourfold community (*caturvidha saṅgha*). The event marks the beginning of the Tīrthaṅkara’s *desanā* (teaching career), lasting until final liberation.

Descriptions of the Samavasaraṇa appear in multiple canonical and post‑canonical texts, often with detailed accounts of its dimensions, the arrangement of auditoriums, the presence of protective deities, and the symbolic flora such as the *aśoka* tree. While Digambara texts emphasize the Tīrthaṅkara’s unclothed state and the absence of images or attendants, Śvetāmbara texts include attendants such as *gaṇadharas* and sometimes depict the Tīrthaṅkara seated beneath a triple canopy. Despite these differences, the core meaning remains consistent: the Samavasaraṇa is the universal preaching hall of perfect knowledge and compassion.

primary_sources.title: Ācārāṅga Sūtra (Śvetāmbara Canon)
primary_sources.author: Traditionally attributed to Mahāvīra’s disciples
primary_sources.notes: The Ācārāṅga Sūtra provides early canonical references to the manifestation of the preaching assembly after omniscience. The description is brief, emphasizing the sacred moment rather than architectural detail.

primary_sources.title: Kalpa Sūtra (Śvetāmbara Mūrti‑pūjaka)
primary_sources.author: Bhadrabāhu (traditionally attributed)
primary_sources.translation: “The Samavasaraṇa was caused to be made by the gods.”
primary_sources.notes: The Kalpa Sūtra gives a narrative account of Mahāvīra’s Samavasaraṇa, including the role of celestial beings and the arrangement of the assembly.

primary_sources.title: Tiloyapaṇṇatti (Digambara)
primary_sources.author: Yativṛṣabha
primary_sources.notes: A detailed cosmological description of the Samavasaraṇa’s structure, dimensions, and arrangement. Digambara texts emphasize symmetry and the universal accessibility of the Tīrthaṅkara’s teaching.

primary_sources.title: Ādi Purāṇa (Digambara)
primary_sources.author: Jinasena
primary_sources.translation: “The divine sound appears to all beings according to their own understanding.”
primary_sources.notes: Although focused on Ṛṣabha, the text includes a general description of the Samavasaraṇa and the nature of the Tīrthaṅkara’s teaching.

misconceptions.myth: The Samavasaraṇa is a human‑constructed temple or building.
misconceptions.reality: Jain texts consistently state that the Samavasaraṇa arises spontaneously through cosmic merit and divine agency, not through human construction.
Primary sources describe attendance by beings from all realms—humans, animals, celestial beings, and even infernal beings who temporarily experience peace.

misconceptions.myth: The Tīrthaṅkara verbally speaks in a human language during the Samavasaraṇa.
misconceptions.reality: Jain doctrine holds that the Tīrthaṅkara emits *divya‑dhvani*, a transcendent sound understood by each being in its own language.

misconceptions.myth: All Jain traditions depict the Samavasaraṇa identically.
misconceptions.reality: While the core concept is shared, Digambara and Śvetāmbara texts differ in details such as attendants, iconography, and architectural features.
